Q: Strange Pylance error on simple Appium-Python-Client setup A:

The two errors occur for different reasons, so I will split the answer into two sections.

"Remote" is not exported from module "appium.webdriver"

The first error occurs because the appium.webdriver module incorrectly declares the Remote symbol as private.

The appium module contains a py.typed marker, which specifies that the module containing it supports type checking functionality. A module containing a py.typed marker is called a py.typed module.

Package maintainers who wish to support type checking of their code MUST add a marker file named py.typed to their package supporting typing. This marker applies recursively: if a top-level package includes it, all its sub-packages MUST support type checking as well.

https://typing.python.org/en/latest/spec/distributing.html#packaging-type-information

For py.typed modules, all imported symbols are considered private by default. To declare an imported symbol as public, it must be re-exported or explicitly declared in __all__.

If a py.typed module is present, a type checker will treat all modules within that package (i.e. all files ending in .py or .pyi) as importable unless the file name begins with an underscore. These modules comprise the supported interface for the library.

Each module exposes a set of symbols. Some of these symbols are considered “private” — implementation details that are not part of the library’s interface. Type checkers can use the following rules to determine which symbols are visible outside of the package.

  • Imported symbols are considered private by default. A fixed set of import forms re-exports imported symbols.
  • A module can expose an __all__ symbol at the module level that provides a list of names considered part of the interface. This overrides all other rules above, allowing imported symbols or symbols whose names begin with an underscore to be included in the interface. (...)

https://typing.python.org/en/latest/spec/distributing.html#library-interface-public-and-private-symbols

Since appium.webdriver is a py.typed module, the imported symbol Remote is considered private. Therefore, when attempting to import and use Remote externally, Pylance raises an error stating that private symbols cannot be imported.

How to Fix

The ideal solution is to add __all__ = ['Remote', 'WebElement'] to appium.webdriver. This makes Remote a public interface, allowing it to be imported without errors. However, it may take time for the package's developer to add this information.

The second method is to ignore the problematic lines using # type: ignore. This temporarily prevents the lines from reporting issues until the problem is resolved.

The final method is to prevent this error from appearing altogether. Add the following line to your user or workspace settings.json. This will ensure the related errors are no longer reported as errors.

    "python.analysis.diagnosticSeverityOverrides": {
        "reportPrivateImportUsage": "none"
    },

You can also change the value from "none" to "information". This allows you to still see the issue, but it won't appear as an error.

Cannot instantiate abstract class "WebDriver"

The second error occurs because Remote does not fully implement the CanExecuteScripts protocol.

Protocols are Python's way of supporting duck typing. If a class implements all the methods required by a specific protocol, it is automatically considered to support that protocol.

However, you can directly inherit from a defined protocol, which allows you to explicitly state that the class supports the protocol.

The Remote class inherits from a protocol named CanExecuteScripts. The protocol is defined as follows:

# appium/protocols/webdriver/can_execute_scripts.py

class CanExecuteScripts(Protocol):
    def pin_script(self, script: str, script_key: Optional[Any] = None) -> Any: ...

    def unpin(self, script_key: Any) -> None: ...

    def get_pinned_scripts(self) -> List[str]: ...

    def execute_script(self, script: str, *args: Any) -> Any: ...

    def execute_async_script(self, script: str, *args: Any) -> Any: ...

To support a protocol, you must define all methods defined in that protocol. However, the Remote class only defines the execute_script method and does not define the remaining four methods.

If a class does not define all elements of a protocol, it is considered an abstract class. Abstract classes cannot be instantiated and used directly; they serve as a foundation for other child classes that fully implement all the protocol's methods.

Since the Remote class does not fully implement the protocol, it is considered an abstract class and therefore cannot be instantiated. Consequently, Pylance raises an error when attempting to instantiate the abstract class Remote.

However, this is not intended when considering the actual implemented code in context. In reality, the methods other than execute_script are neither used nor defined anywhere. Therefore, even if these four methods are not implemented, no issues arise at runtime as long as a user does not attempt to use not implemented methods.

In this case, the developer's responsibility is more pronounced. While the first error was a corner case that could be easily overlooked if not properly addressed, this case directly contradicts the intended usage of the protocol.

How to Fix

The solution is similar. Developers can either properly implement the remaining four methods or remove the unimplemented protocol. You can add # type: ignore to the lines causing errors or disable Pylance's reportAbstractUsage diagnostic.

EDIT: I submitted a PR to resolve these issues.

Q: How to rename a "broken" view A:

SSMS basically does an sp_rename under the hood. That works even on broken views because it just updates the name in sys.objects without validating the body.

EXEC sp_rename 'dbo.vw_t_dummy', 'z_vw_t_dummy';

The catch is that sp_rename won't touch the view definition (as you noticed), so after renaming you still need to fix it with ALTER VIEW:

ALTER VIEW dbo.z_vw_t_dummy AS
SELECT i
FROM t_dummy;
GO

Your CREATE VIEW probably failed because the SELECT still referenced the dropped column z, not because of the rename itself. If you just want a clean cut you can also drop the broken view and recreate it with the new name. Either way you'll have to update the column list.

Hope that helps!

Q: Apply a SQL Case condition to a SQL duplicated row in the same statement A:

The problem is in your new SQL, as follows:

In this clause...

INSERT INTO myrota (weekstart)

...you've told it you're going to insert one column, but then your SELECT statement includes two columns (both of which have the same alias!):

That should be producing a SQL error when you execute it

Column count doesn't match value count

Demo: https://dbfiddle.uk/-HgFidNC. If you didn't see that error then either a) you didn't actually execute the query or b) you've suppressed your error reporting for some reason (which is never good idea, especially not while testing) or c) you're looking in the wrong place for error messages, perhaps.

Assuming you wanted to replace the static reference to weekstart with the output of the CASE statement, then just remove the original weekstart reference from the query:

INSERT INTO myrota (weekstart)
SELECT
  CASE
       WHEN weekstart= '2026-03-02' THEN '2026-03-16'
       WHEN weekstart= '2026-03-09' THEN  '2026-03-23'
       ELSE 'empty'
  END AS weekstart
FROM myrota

Now you are only outputting one column again, which matches the column list in the INSERT clause.

This would have been a lot easier for you to understand, research and solve if your PHP side was reporting the errors propery, and/or if you tested the query indepdently in SQL directly beforehand, to ensure the basic structure is right. Make sure you have a look at How can I get useful error messages in PHP? to ensure your PHP setup is correct.

Q: Warning in R 'is not a factor variable' in package marked A:

I had the same problem, found the answer here: http://www.phidot.org/forum/viewtopic.php?f=21&t=3876

in short, readxl creates a tibble, not a data frame, which makes it read the variable wrong.

try:

gm.db <- as.data.frame(gm.db)

This fixed it for me.

Q: Wrong operator<< selected depending on whether a member function is called A:

I don't know why the overload selection is made as such, but thanks to @NathanOliver I found an explanation and a workaround:

The usage of the member function doesn't matter here.

The inline overload is always selected because it is preferred against the const & one, and then a compile error occurs because there is no suitable append() overload.

To force the use of the correct operator I added this version of append() to the Builder class:

template<typename T, typename = std::enable_if_t<std::is_class_v<T>>>
Builder & append(T const & t) { return *this << t; }
